## Concepts covered

**[Optimisation methods](../../concepts/optimizer-adam-adamw-sgd.md)** — the subject of the work. The question is posed thus: why is SGD better than Adam on a ResNet while on a ViT it is the other way round ([`p2-1`](#p2-1), [`tab-1`](#tab-1))? The answer is sought neither in the architecture of the network nor in the learning rate but in two quantities taken from the Hessian: the sharpness (its trace) and the **entropy gap** ([`p3-1`](#p3-1)).

**[Progress measures](../../concepts/progress-measures.md)** — a new one is proposed: the entropy gap $\ln n - \operatorname{H}(H)$ for a Hessian $H$ of size $n\times n$, where $\operatorname{H}$ is the von Neumann matrix entropy ([`p2-2`](#p2-2), [`p3-1`](#p3-1)). The argument against sharpness alone is direct: it sets the **overall** speed of escape from a saddle but says nothing about its **uniformity** across directions ([`p3-2`](#p3-2)).

**[Spectral analysis](../../concepts/spectral-analysis-svd-esd-fve.md)** — the entropy gap is in essence a measure of the non-uniformity of the Hessian spectrum. Theorem 2.2 relates it to the condition number $k$: $\log n-\operatorname{H}_{1}(\mathbf{H})\leq\frac{k}{k+n-1}\log k-\log\frac{n+k-1}{n}\leq\log k$ ([`p3-4`](#p3-4)), whence a large gap forces a large condition number, and that slows the convergence ([`p3-5`](#p3-5)).

**[The loss landscape and basins](../../concepts/loss-landscape-basins.md)** — the starting consideration is taken from Xie et al. 2022: the displacement from a saddle along eigen-direction $i$ is $\Delta\theta_{i}^{2}\sim O(|\lambda_{i}|)$ ([`p3-2`](#p3-2)). A small entropy gap means that the network escapes the saddle well **in all** directions at once.

**[Generalisation bounds](../../concepts/generalization-bounds.md)** — the second support. The posterior distribution is approximated by the Laplace $\mathcal{N}(\theta^{ * },(H+\sigma^{-2}I)^{-1})$ ([`p5-2`](#p5-2)), after which a PAC-Bayes bound is written out explicitly, and three quantities enter it: the norm $\Vert\theta^{ * }\Vert$, the trace of the Hessian and the entropy gap ([`p6-1`](#p6-1)). The progress measure is thereby derived rather than guessed at.

**[The total variation distance](../../concepts/manifold-representation-compression.md)** — the auxiliary lemmas 2.5 and 2.6 bound the entropy gap through the total variation distance to the uniform distribution: $\ln n-H(a)\leq n\Vert a-u\Vert_{TV}$ ([`p6-10`](#p6-10), [`p8-2`](#p8-2)). This translates the "non-uniformity of the spectrum" into a language in which it is easy to compute.

**[Real-task data](../../concepts/vision-real-world-data-mnist-cifar.md)** — the whole experimental part: CIFAR10, a ResNet18 and a ViT, the methods SGD and Adam, six points along the training ([`tab-1`](#tab-1)). On the ResNet18 SGD gives 95.21 % against Adam's 93.53 %, on the ViT 83.23 % against 87.21 % ([`tab-1`](#tab-1)); and the sharpness of Adam on the ResNet is forty times larger ([`tab-3`](#tab-3)) while the entropy gap is three times larger ([`tab-4`](#tab-4)).

**[The coefficient of variation](../../concepts/heavy-tailed-self-regularization-htsr.md)** — a third measure: the deviation of the entropy across the blocks of the network ([`tab-5`](#tab-5)). Theorem 2.7 shows that for independent samples from $\mathcal{N}(a,b^{2})$ the entropy of the ratios $|x_{i}|/\sum|x_{i}|$ behaves as $\log n-O(b^{2}/a^{2})$, where $b/a$ is precisely the coefficient of variation ([`p9-2`](#p9-2)). The method with the better quality invariably has the **smaller** deviation across the blocks ([`p9-1`](#p9-1)).

**[The compression of representations](../../concepts/manifold-representation-compression.md)** — the second half of the work. The Lion update rule, $\theta_{t}\leftarrow\theta_{t-1}-\eta_{t}\cdot\operatorname{sign}(U_{t})$ ([`p9-4`](#p9-4)), is read as a **compressor of information about the update direction**: each component of $U_{t}$ encodes the "true" direction $Y\in\lbrace+1,-1\rbrace$, and $\operatorname{sign}$ is the Bayes-optimal classifier for such a problem ([`p9-6`](#p9-6), [`p10-1`](#p10-1)).

**[Effective theory and statistical physics](../../concepts/effective-theory-statistical-mechanics.md)** — from the information bottleneck (IB) and from the maximum-entropy principle one and the same thing is derived by two routes: the optimal representation is $T=\tanh(\mu x/\sigma^{2})$ rather than $\operatorname{sign}(x)$ ([`p12-1`](#p12-1), [`p12-13`](#p12-13)). Hence the proposal to improve Lion by replacing the sign with a hyperbolic tangent ([`p11-3`](#p11-3)).

**[Grokking](../../concepts/grokking.md)** — it is **never once mentioned** in the work. It entered the corpus by adjacency: the same author wrote "Understanding Grokking Through A Robustness Viewpoint" (2311.06597), in which the progress measure is likewise built out of information theory — there a pairwise mutual information, here the entropy of the Hessian. A kinship of method, not of subject.

Cards of corpus papers: [Tan & Huang 2023](../../papers/2311.06597.understanding-grokking-through-a-robustness-viewpoint/2311.06597.understanding-grokking-through-a-robustness-viewpoint.card.md) — the same author's work on grokking, in which the progress measure is built out of information theory; [Clauw, Stramaglia, Marinazzo 2024](../../papers/2408.08944.information-theoretic-progress-measures-reveal-grokking-is-an-emergent-phase-transition/2408.08944.information-theoretic-progress-measures-reveal-grokking-is-an-emergent-phase-transition.card.md) — progress measures through the O-information, the nearest in conception; [Beck et al. 2024](../../papers/2410.04489.grokking-at-the-edge-of-linear-separability/2410.04489.grokking-at-the-edge-of-linear-separability.card.md) — critical slowing down, in which the convergence rate likewise runs into the conditioning.

## What is shown and what is conjectured

The card editor's remarks following the analysis of the claims (`…claims.txt`). The work is short: thirteen pages, half of them derivations; not a single figure, and five tables of four rows each.

**The measure is chosen sensibly and derived rather than assigned.** The entropy gap appears in the PAC-Bayes bound alongside the norm and the trace of the Hessian ([`p6-1`](#p6-1)) — that is, it is not a rule of thumb but a term of the bound. For a corpus in which progress measures are many and derived ones may be counted on one hand, this is valuable.

**The argument against sharpness alone is put precisely.** The sharpness sets the overall speed of escape from a saddle, the entropy gap its uniformity across directions ([`p3-2`](#p3-2)). The two quantities measure different things, and the tables presented confirm it: for Adam on the ResNet the trace of the Hessian is forty times larger and the entropy gap three times ([`tab-3`](#tab-3), [`tab-4`](#tab-4)).

**The relation to the condition number is proved rather than claimed.** Theorem 2.2 gives a closed-form bound, and the proof is carried through to the end by an enumeration of the "extremal" distributions ([`p3-6`](#p3-6)–[`p4-12`](#p4-12)).

**The deviation across the blocks is an observation in its own right.** The method with the better quality is invariably more uniform across the blocks ([`p9-1`](#p9-1), [`tab-5`](#tab-5)), and theorem 2.7 relates this to the coefficient of variation ([`p9-2`](#p9-2)).

**The reading of Lion as an information compressor is elegant.** The $\operatorname{sign}$ function turns out to be the Bayes-optimal classifier for a Gaussian two-class problem ([`p10-1`](#p10-1)), and the IB and the maximum-entropy principle give $\tanh$ by two independent routes ([`p12-1`](#p12-1), [`p12-13`](#p12-13)).

**The main claim, however — "we find ways to improve Lion" — is never once checked.** Replacing $\operatorname{sign}$ with $\tanh$ is proposed ([`p11-3`](#p11-3)) and derived, but there is **not a single experiment with it in the work**: no table, not a line about accuracy. The abstract promises an improvement, the text gives only an argument.

**The experimental part is four points.** One dataset (CIFAR10), two architectures, two optimisation methods; no number of seeds, no spread, no confidence intervals ([`tab-1`](#tab-1)–[`tab-5`](#tab-5)). On four points the statement "a smaller entropy gap corresponds to better quality" is indistinguishable from a coincidence.

**The entropy gap is computed not for the whole Hessian but block by block.** How exactly the network is divided into blocks, how many there are and how the values are combined into a single number is said nowhere; table 2 speaks of "the fraction of positive Hessians among the blocks" ([`tab-2`](#tab-2)), that is, there are dozens of blocks, but there is no definition of them.

**The bound of theorem 2.4 is written out with a misprint.** The brackets do not match inside the radical, and the quantity $\sigma^{2}+\mu$ adds the variance of the prior distribution to the smallest eigenvalue of the Hessian ([`p6-1`](#p6-1)) — quantities of different natures. The proof is not carried through to that expression: it breaks off at the Kullback–Leibler divergence ([`p6-4`](#p6-4)).

**The text is unproofread.** The section "2. Maximum Entropy Optimization" ([`p12-3`](#p12-3)) stands with no first section; in lemma 2.5 the reference to an equation is printed as "14" without brackets ([`p6-7`](#p6-7)); the "Related Works" section fits into three sentences and stands **after** the conclusion ([`p13-3`](#p13-3)); and the arXiv submission is assembled from two main files, one of which has retained the title of the author's earlier paper (see the note on the source above).

**Its place in the corpus.** There is not a word about grokking here, and there is no point pretending otherwise: the work entered the collection by adjacency of method, not of subject. Two things are valuable: a measure of the non-uniformity of the Hessian spectrum **derived** from a PAC-Bayes bound, and the observation that the better optimisation method is the more uniform across the blocks of the network. Both are usable as progress measures where sharpness is taken today. The price: four experiments, no spread, no definition of the blocks, and the promised improvement of Lion never checked at all.

###### p1-2

Optimizers are critical to the success of neural network training, dictating how quickly and effectively a model converges to a solution. While several optimizers, such as SGD, and Adam are widely used, understanding why certain optimizers outperform others on specific architectures remains a challenge. Traditional methods for analyzing optimizers, such as sharpness metrics based on the Hessian matrix, offer valuable insights into the local landscape around minima or saddle points but fail to fully capture the underlying optimization dynamics.

In this paper, we extend the analysis of optimizer behavior by introducing the concept in information theory. The entropy gap of the hessian provides more details of the optimizer's trajectory during training, offering an additional lens through which to examine convergence behavior and generalization. Along with sharpness, the entropy gap captures more local curvature statistics along optimization steps, shedding light on how optimizers traverse the loss surface and escape from saddle points.

We then apply information-theoretic tools to analyze the Lion optimizer's update rule, a recent addition to the family of optimizers. The Lion optimizer has gained attention for its simplicity and effectiveness, yet its effectiveness is still not fully understood. By incorporating tools like mutual information into the analysis of Lion, we uncover new insights into its optimization dynamics. Specifically, we show that it can be seen as an effective update direction information compressor. We further use these tools to help improve Lion.

Through detailed experiments and theoretical analysis, we demonstrate that both sharpness and entropy gap significantly affect the performance of different optimizers. By examining the training dynamics of popular architectures like ResNet and ViT under different optimizers, we highlight the importance of considering both metrics when evaluating optimizer effectiveness.

This work offers a deeper, more nuanced understanding of optimizer behavior, providing a new avenue for designing and analyzing optimization algorithms. By bridging the gap between information theory and optimization dynamics, we propose a more robust framework for optimizer evaluation and improvement, which **[p. 2]** may also be applied to a wide range of other topics. Our findings contribute to the growing body of knowledge in optimization theory, suggesting that careful consideration of information-theoretic tools can lead to more efficient and generalizable optimization strategies.

###### p2-1

In this paper, we consider the training dynamics of different optimizers on different architectures, which include ResNet and ViT under SGD and Adam. During training, we can see that ResNet has a better landscape compared to ViT, making SGD behaves better than Adam on ResNet but vice versa on ViT. However, the sharpness (trace of hessian) cannot fully explain this behavior, making us consider new metrics like the entropy gap.

###### p2-2

Suppose a positive semi-definite matrix $\mathbf{R} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ which $\mathbf{R}(i,i)=1$ for every $i=1, \cdots, n$ and $\alpha>0$. The $\alpha$-order (Rényi) entropy for matrix $\mathbf{R}$ is defined as follows: $$
\operatorname{H}_\alpha\left(\mathbf{R}\right)=\frac{1}{1-\alpha} \log \left[\operatorname{tr}\left(\left(\frac{1}{n} \mathbf{R} \right)^\alpha\right)\right],
$$ where $\mathbf{R}^{\alpha}$ is the matrix power. The case of $\alpha=1$ recovers the von Neumann (matrix) entropy, i.e., $$
\operatorname{H}_1\left(\mathbf{R}\right)=-\operatorname{tr}\left(\frac{1}{n} \mathbf{R} \log \frac{1}{n} \mathbf{R} \right).
$$

**[p. 3]**

###### p3-1

In this paper, if not stated otherwise, we will always use $\alpha=1$. And the entropy gap will be $\ln n - \operatorname{H}(H)$ of a p.s.d. matrix $H$ of size $n \times n$.

###### p3-2

From (Xie et al., 2022), we know that during optimization displacement from a saddle point along eigen-direction $i$ is $\Delta \theta_i^2 \sim O(|\lambda_i|)$, where $\lambda_i$ is the eigenvalue of hessian. Then it is clear that two values matter for the escape from saddle point speed: 1. The sharpness (trace of hessian) quantifies the total speed of escaping 2. The entropy gap $\log n - \operatorname{H}_1(\mathbf{H})$ measures the «uniformness» of escaping. A small gap will ensure the network escapes from the saddle point well in all directions.

The hessian entropy has a close relationship with the condition number of hessian, which directly relates to the convergence speed of optimization.

###### p3-4

Suppose the Hessian matrix $\mathbf{H} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ is positive definite and $k$ is the condition number of it, then the following bound holds: $\log n - \operatorname{H}_1(\mathbf{H}) \leq \frac{k}{k+n-1} \log k - \log \frac{n+k-1}{n}  \leq \log k$.

###### p3-5

From theorem 2.2, it is clear a big entropy gap $\log n - \operatorname{H}_1(\mathbf{H})$ may force the network to have a big condition number. So a smaller gap is favorable for faster convergence of training.

###### p3-6

We aim to prove that among all probability distributions satisfying the constraints:

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i = 1, \quad \frac{a_{\max}}{a_{\min}} \leq k, \tag{1}
$$

the entropy

$$
H(\mathbf{a}) = -\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i \ln a_i \tag{2}
$$

achieves its minimum value only for the following «extreme» distribution:

$$
\exists i_0: \quad a_{i_0} = M, \quad \forall j \neq i_0: \quad a_j = m, \tag{3}
$$

where

$$
\frac{M}{m} = k, \quad M + (n-1)m = 1. \tag{4}
$$

The proof consists of two parts:

- Prove that any «non-extreme» pair of elements can be adjusted to strictly decrease entropy.

- Conclude that the minimum entropy distribution must be the unique form where only one element attains the maximum value while all others take the same minimum value.

###### p4-12

Then calculating the entropy value will give the final bound.

**[p. 5]**

###### p5-2

Let the likelihood function of the dataset $\mathcal{D}$ be $P(\mathcal{D}|\theta)$, with the corresponding negative log-likelihood function $\mathcal{L}(\theta) = -\log P(\mathcal{D}|\theta)$, and assume a Gaussian prior distribution $P(\theta) = \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 I)$. Then, the posterior distribution can be approximated by $$P(\theta|\mathcal{D}) \approx \mathcal{N}\left(\theta^*, \left(H + \frac{1}{\sigma^2} I\right)^{-1}\right),$$ where $H$ is the hessian.

###### p5-8

We can now present a PAC-Bayes generalization bound which shows what metrics of the network mainly affect generalization.

1. **Empirical Loss and Its Expectation:** Let $\hat{L}(\theta)$ denote the empirical (training) loss at parameter $\theta$. For any distribution $Q$ over the parameter space, define $$\hat{L}(Q) = \mathbb{E}_{\theta \sim Q}[\hat{L}(\theta)].$$ When the training set is sufficiently large and $Q$ is concentrated near $\theta^*$, we approximate $$\hat{L}(Q) \approx \hat{L}(\theta^*) \approx L(\theta^*).$$

**[p. 6]**

1. **PAC-Bayes Inequality:** For a training set of size $n$, the PAC-Bayes framework guarantees that, with probability at least $1-\delta$ (for any $\delta\in(0,1)$), $$\mathbb{E}_{\theta\sim Q}[L(\theta)] \le \hat{L}(Q) + \sqrt{\frac{KL(Q\|P)+\ln\frac{1}{\delta}}{2n}}.$$

###### p6-1

Assume that there exists a local minimizer $\theta^* \in \mathbb{R}^d$ of the true loss function $L(\theta)$ with positive definite Hessian $H$ and $\mu I \preccurlyeq H$. Let the prior and posterior be defined by $$P = \mathcal{N}(0,\,\sigma^2 I), \quad Q = \mathcal{N}\Big(\theta^*,\, \left(H + \frac{1}{\sigma^2} I\right)^{-1}\Big),$$ and assume that the empirical risk under $Q$ satisfies $\hat{L}(Q) \approx L(\theta^*)$. Then, for any $\delta \in (0,1)$ and for a training set of size $n$, with probability at least $1-\delta$, the following generalization bound holds: $$\begin{aligned}&\mathbb{E}_{\theta\sim Q}[L(\theta)] -  L(\theta^*)  \\
&\leq \sqrt{\frac{1}{2n} (\ln \frac{1}{\delta} + d \ln( \frac{\sigma^2 + \mu}{d}) + \frac{\|\theta^*\|^2}{\sigma^2} + d (\ln \operatorname{tr}(H) + (\ln d - \operatorname{H}(H) ) - \frac{1}{d}(\ln d - \operatorname{H}(H) )^2 ) }.\end{aligned}$$

###### p6-4

Therefore, the KL divergence is $$KL(Q\|P) = \frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\operatorname{tr}\Big(\left(H + \frac{1}{\sigma^2} I\right)^{-1}\Big) + \frac{\|\theta^*\|^2}{\sigma^2} - d + d\ln\sigma^2 + \ln\det\left(H + \frac{1}{\sigma^2} I\right)\right].$$

###### p6-7

Since $$\sum_{i=1}^n\left(\frac{1}{n}-a_i\right)=0,$$ we partition the index set into $$I := \{i: a_i<1/n\} \quad \text{and} \quad J := \{i: a_i>1/n\}.$$ Thus, we can rewrite 14 as $$A - B = \sum_{i\in I}\left(\frac{1}{n}-a_i\right)(-\ln a_i)
+\sum_{j\in J}\left(\frac{1}{n}-a_j\right)(-\ln a_j).$$ Note that for $j\in J$ we have $\frac{1}{n}-a_j<0$, so that $$A-B = \sum_{i\in I}\left(\frac{1}{n}-a_i\right)(-\ln a_i)
-\sum_{j\in J}\left(a_j-\frac{1}{n}\right)(-\ln a_j).$$

Since the function $-\ln x$ is monotone decreasing (because $\ln x$ is increasing), we have: $$\text{For } i\in I:\quad -\ln a_i \ge -\ln a_{\min},$$ and $$\text{For } j\in J:\quad -\ln a_j \le -\ln a_{\max},$$ where $$a_{\min} := \min\{a_1,\dots,a_n\} \quad \text{and} \quad a_{\max} := \max\{a_1,\dots,a_n\}.$$ Thus, for every $i\in I$, $$\left(\frac{1}{n}-a_i\right)(-\ln a_i) \ge \left(\frac{1}{n}-a_i\right)(-\ln a_{\min}),$$ and for every $j\in J$, $$\left(a_j-\frac{1}{n}\right)(-\ln a_j) \le \left(a_j-\frac{1}{n}\right)(-\ln a_{\max}).$$

Let $$C := \sum_{i\in I}\left(\frac{1}{n}-a_i\right) = \sum_{j\in J}\left(a_j-\frac{1}{n}\right)=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^n \left|a_i - \frac{1}{n}\right|,$$ **[p. 7]** where the equality follows from the fact that $\sum_{i=1}^n (\frac{1}{n}-a_i)=0$. Then, combining the above estimates, we obtain $$A-B \ge C\Bigl[(-\ln a_{\min})-(-\ln a_{\max})\Bigr]
= C\ln\frac{a_{\max}}{a_{\min}}.$$

**[p. 8]**

###### p6-10

By noticing $C = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^n \left|a_i - \frac{1}{n}\right|$, define $u = \left(\frac{1}{n}, \frac{1}{n}, \dots, \frac{1}{n}\right)$ be the uniform distribution. We have the following relationship: $$\|a-u\|_{TV} = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^n \left|a_i - \frac{1}{n}\right|,$$ where TV is the total variation distance.

Then we can conclude that,

###### p8-2

$\ln n - H(a) \le n\,\|a-u\|_{TV}.$

###### p9-1

We find that for SGD and Adam, the better performance optimizer for each architecture has a smaller deviation among blocks, showing a more uniform structure, which also relates to the coefficient of variation.

###### p9-2

Suppose $x_i$ ($i=1, \cdots,n$) are i.i.d. random samples taken from $\mathcal{N}(a, b^2)$, where $a>0$. Then $-\sum^n_{i=1} \frac{|x_i|}{\sum^n_{i=1} |x_i|} \log \frac{|x_i|}{\sum^n_{i=1} |x_i|} \sim \log n - O(\frac{b^2}{a^2})$, where $\frac{b}{a}$ is often called the coefficient of variation.

###### p9-4

*Algorithm 1: Lion Optimizer*
```
Input: Parameters $\theta_t-1$, momentum $m_0=0$, gradients $\nabla \theta_t$, learning rate $\eta_t$, momenta $\beta_1$, $\beta_2$
For $t = 1 \dots T$
$U_t \gets \beta_2 m_t-1 + (1 - \beta_2) \nabla \theta_t$
$\theta_t \gets \theta_t-1 - \eta_t \cdot sign(U_t)$
$m_t \gets \beta_1 m_t-1 + (1 - \beta_1)\nabla \theta_t$
```

As the previous sections discuss the information dynamics of training of some optimizers, it is interested to see that can information theory be used to analyze the update rule and improve it. In this section, we will focus on a new optimizer called Lion.

###### p9-6

To model this optimizer's behavior, we consider each component of its $U_t$ encodes a «true» update direction $Y$ and transform the problem as follows.

###### p10-1

Under Definition 3.1, the Bayes optimal classifier is: $$f^*(X) = \text{\rm sign}(X),$$ with the decision rule: $$f^*(X) =
\begin{cases}
+1 & \text{if } X \geq 0, \\
-1 & \text{if } X < 0.
\end{cases}$$

###### p11-3

We can use the tanh function to improve the optimizer.

Recall the binary classification problem where the output $Y \in \{+1, -1\}$ and the input $X$ satisfies the following conditions: $$X \mid Y = +1 \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2), \quad X \mid Y = -1 \sim \mathcal{N}(-\mu, \sigma^2),$$ with equal priors for both classes: $$p(Y = +1) = p(Y = -1) = \frac{1}{2}.$$

The goal is to find an optimal representation $T$ of $X$ in the Information Bottleneck (IB) framework, where the representation $T$ compresses $X$ as much as possible while retaining information about $Y$. Strictly speaking, this problem is formulated as: $$\min_{p(t \mid x)} \, I(X; T) - \beta I(T; Y),$$ where $\beta > 0$ is a regularization parameter controlling the trade-off between compression and information retention.

In the IB framework, we aim to maximize $I(T; Y)$ while minimizing $I(X; T)$. The optimal representation $T$ is the one that maximizes the mutual information with $Y$ while keeping the mutual information with $X$ small, subject to a constraint.

To find the optimal $T$, we can use the following: $$T = \arg \max_T I(T; Y) \quad \text{subject to} \quad I(X; T) \leq C,$$ where $C$ is the compression constraint.

In a binary classification problem, the posterior probability $p(Y \mid X)$ is a sufficient statistic for $X$ with respect to $Y$. Using Bayes' theorem, the posterior probability is given by: $$p(Y = +1 \mid X = x) = \frac{p(X = x \mid Y = +1) p(Y = +1)}{p(X = x)}.$$ Since the conditional distributions are Gaussian, the log-likelihood ratio $r(x)$ is: $$r(x) = \log \frac{p(x \mid Y = +1)}{p(x \mid Y = -1)} = \frac{2\mu}{\sigma^2} x.$$ Thus, the posterior probability $p(Y = +1 \mid x)$ becomes: $$p(Y = +1 \mid x) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(-r(x))} = \frac{1}{1 + \exp\left(- \frac{2\mu}{\sigma^2} x \right)}.$$ We can express the posterior expectation $E[Y \mid x]$ as: $$E[Y \mid x] = 2 p(Y = +1 \mid x) - 1 = \tanh\left(\frac{r(x)}{2}\right) = \tanh\left(\frac{\mu}{\sigma^2} x\right).$$

**[p. 12]**

###### p12-1

In the IB problem, we aim to compress $X$ while retaining information about $Y$. According to information theory, for a set of variables satisfying the Markov chain $Y \to X \to T$, the unique $T$ that satisfies $I(T; Y) = I(X; Y)$ (i.e., perfectly preserving the information about $Y$) is the sufficient statistic. Therefore, the optimal $T$ is $T = \tanh\left( \frac{\mu}{\sigma^2} x \right)$.

We can also derive the $\tanh$ function from a maximal entropy principle. Consider a binary random variable $Y \in \{+1, -1\}$. Under the constraint $\mathbb{E}[Y] = \mu$, we derive its maximum entropy distribution.

###### p12-3

Maximize the entropy $H(p) = -\sum_{y} p(y) \ln p(y)$, subject to:

- Normalization: $p(+1) + p(-1) = 1$

- Expectation constraint: $p(+1) - p(-1) = \mu$

Construct the Lagrangian:

$$
\mathcal{L} = -\sum_{y} p(y) \ln p(y) + x \left( p(+1) - p(-1) - \mu \right) + \lambda \left( p(+1) + p(-1) - 1 \right)
$$

where $x$ and $\lambda$ are Lagrange multipliers.

Differentiate with respect to $p(+1)$ and $p(-1)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial p(+1)} &= -\ln p(+1) - 1 + x + \lambda = 0 \implies \ln p(+1) = x + \lambda - 1 \\
    \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial p(-1)} &= -\ln p(-1) - 1 - x + \lambda = 0 \implies \ln p(-1) = -x + \lambda - 1\end{aligned}
$$

Thus: $$p(+1) = e^{x + \lambda - 1}, \quad p(-1) = e^{-x + \lambda - 1}$$

Using $p(+1) + p(-1) = 1$:

$$
\begin{aligned}&e^{x + \lambda - 1} + e^{-x + \lambda - 1} = 1 \\
    &e^{\lambda - 1}(e^x + e^{-x}) = 1 \\
    &e^{\lambda - 1} = \frac{1}{2\cosh(x)} \quad \text{(since $e^x + e^{-x} = 2\cosh(x)$)}\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute $\lambda$: $$p(+1) = \frac{e^x}{2\cosh(x)}, \quad p(-1) = \frac{e^{-x}}{2\cosh(x)}$$ Unified form: $$p(y; x) = \frac{e^{x y}}{2\cosh(x)}, \quad y \in \{+1, -1\}$$

Calculate $\mathbb{E}[Y] = \mu$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu &= \frac{e^x}{2\cosh(x)}(+1) + \frac{e^{-x}}{2\cosh(x)}(-1) \\
        &= \frac{e^x - e^{-x}}{2\cosh(x)} \\
        &= \frac{\sinh(x)}{\cosh(x)} = \tanh(x)\end{aligned}
$$

**[p. 13]**

###### p12-13

Thus $\mu = \tanh(x)$.

###### p13-3

Information theory has long served as a powerful tool for analyzing the relationship between probability and information. It has been applied to gain insights into the inner workings of neural networks (Tishby et al., 2000; Tishby & Zaslavsky, 2015), aiming to make their operations more interpretable, akin to a "white-box" approach. However, due to the high computational cost of traditional information-theoretic measures, recent research has shifted towards extending these concepts to assess relationships between matrices (Bach, 2022; Skean et al., 2023; Zhang et al.(2023 b); Zhang et al.(2023 a)). In this context, Tan et al., 2023 utilize matrix mutual information and joint entropy in the field of self-supervised learning.
